title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth — the Farthest Any Human Object Has Flown

content:
NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth — about 16.1 billion miles away, a distance so great that a radio signal now takes a full day to reach it.

The spacecraft crossed the threshold at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, Nov. 18, after more than 49 years of constant travel since its launch in 1977. Because of the distance, NASA did not confirm the milestone until Thursday, when the signal verifying it arrived.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours — about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers), more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto. Any command NASA sends now needs roughly 24 hours just to reach Voyager 1, and another full day to hear back.

The milestone is an engineering feat rather than a scientific one: the spacecraft is doing nothing different, and the crossing changes nothing about how it operates. But it marks the farthest any object built by humans has ever flown.

Voyager 1 is traveling at nearly 38,000 mph through interstellar space, still sending back data. It is headed in the direction of a star known as Gliese 445, more than 17 light-years away. At its current pace, it would take about 18,000 years to travel a full light-year.

Its twin, Voyager 2, is trailing behind at more than 13.4 billion miles from Earth, with messages taking about 20 hours to arrive. It is on pace to reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035. NASA expects Voyager 1 to keep communicating until its power runs out, around 2036.
